doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Social forces, spirit and jazz history; meeting Sangeeta
summary: Debate over social causes of musical change, James Reese Europe in France and spiritual views of playing, ending with how he met Sangeeta in the street.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: In that film, and in other places, when I read about jazz, I sometimes object to the idea that changes in music, jazz especially, are often because of social issues. To me they leave out the thing about people just experiment because they can, and because it feels good to do something new, or — Evan Christopher, who’s a clarinetist we’ve had at the college, had this interesting theory about why vibrato with the early New Orleans clarinetists, and it had to do with playing with out of tune pianos. You know, that kind.
Wait a minute. There’s vibrato and there’s vibrato. You have the vibrato of the clarinetist and then you have Sidney Bechet, which brought vibrato to a whole other level. He made vibrato an art form.
I’m not sure I agree with that. I think that — did you ever read a book called — we were talking about this, how both of us are losing things — Jazz: A People’s Music?
I think I did. LeRoi Jones?

No, no, no, no, no. It’s a Marxist historian. It’s a very interesting book. It’s about music and social change and I found it a fascinating book when I read it. And I also think that if you look at the arts, I think everything is interconnected. I think that World War II, there was an innocence pre-World War II. World War II came, with the advent of the bomb, and with a sense all of us made for the first time that we could face extinction. That gave rise to a different form of literature, the existentialist writings and I think music changed also. There’s another thing, I really believe this, look at Bird and Dizzy, who were just phenomenal technicians. Now these are musicians who might have tried out for symphony orchestras but — would have wanted to try out for symphony orchestras but they never would get a chance. So whether it was conscious or unconscious, they developed their chops to an unbelievable degree. And then they had these cutting sessions and they’d take tempos at 320 or something like that, and say, “Okay white boy, come in and try to — you think you’re such good players, try to play this.” So whether that’s a conscious force or any unconscious force — or take what happened in World War I, when the 369th regiment band, James Reese Europe’s marching band came and they went to Europe, and they played in France, and they swung. And the French people responded,

partially because France was a colonial power. And they had a percent of African music in their DNA almost, let alone within their culture. So they saw black musicians as a carrier of a tradition from Africa, whereas America looked at black musicians as, what was jazz, this was like a sexual act. It was like lowbrow music. It was — oh it doesn’t qualify — all the rants against jazz will deprave you, it’ll make your children depraved, and all that stuff. But in France they recognized this music as an offshoot to African music. And the black musicians — women threw themselves at them, people brought them drinks, and a lot of them stayed after the war was over, in Paris and in France in general and in Europe, and they invited their friends to come over. And then the first jazz criticism was written by Frenchmen. And they helped Americans appreciate their own art form. So I don’t think musical development or any art form — there were people in the Vanguard who were ahead of the curve — like Bird was or Coltrane — but some of that’s spiritual. I think they’re in touch with the spiritual. You know you listen to a lot of musicians, and writers say this too and painters, some of they say, “It’s not me that’s doing the playing, this is something that passes through me.” I tune my own instrument, my body, my technique, just like you make a radio as pure as you can to receive transmissions that come through it. You make your own instrument as pure as you can so what comes through from some other planet or wherever music comes from, passes through you. It’s amazing how many quote famous musicians would say it’s not me playing, I’m just passing it on. So I think it’s all connected — history and social movements and spiritual stuff, and there are so many factors that come into play. I’m doing this film on this musician with Parkinson’s. I met him in the street and after talking to him for an hour I just got this message, I’ve got to make the film on this guy. I mean he lives in California but he happened to be here because he used to live here and he was visiting. I was talking in the street with Marc Black who is the musician that Warren was talking about who plays so loud sometimes. And here’s how things interconnect. We were talking about a Warren Bernhardt concert. Warren had just gave a concert at the Kleinert. And we were talking on the street about the concert the night before. I actually remember this. We were talking about the Rachmaninoff preludes. Apparently there are twenty-four. I didn’t know this. And Marc was saying there are twenty-four because each one is in every key in the major and minor of every key and that’s why there are twenty- four. And Sangeeta was sitting on a bench and he was looking at us and he’s in his seventies and he’s small and he was looking at us. And he got up and said — he sort of walked funny and came over and says, “Excuse me, you guys talking about music?” And we said yeah.
